title: About meteocool
text1: meteocool is a free GIS visualisation & aggregation platform with focus on severe weather. Optimized for mobile devices, you can use it to both chase or avoid upcoming weather - that's up to you.
text2: meteocool currently uses radar data provided by DWD, realtime lightning information from the awesome blitzortung.org project and satellite imagery from the EC/ESA Copernicus Programme.

features.list0: No user accounts are required to use the application, no location data will be recorded or used for other purposes. See also our Privacy Policy.
features.list1: The biggest inconvenience with most weather radar visualizations is out-of-date data. meteocool notifies its clients as soon as new radar data becomes available and is always ready for you with up-to-date data.
features.list2: New lightning strikes are displayed instantly, giving you an even better feeling for the cloud formation's intensity, trajectory and speed.
features.list3: Get notified about incoming rain and severe weather up to 60 minutes in advance. This works on the web and is available for iOS and Android as well. You can even set the notification level to your liking to only get notified if there's heavy rain for example.
features.list4: Native iOS and Android apps provide battery-efficient background location services to allow for accurate weather notifications everywhere you go
features.list5: meteocool offers a dark and light theme to adapt to your preferences.

settings.title: Settings
settings.color_map_hint: Changes the colors the precipitation is drawn in.
settings.rotation_hint: Only on the 2D map. The 3D map always takes the full set of touch gestures, rotating and tilting included.
settings.solid_glass_hint: Makes the frosted panels over the map solid while you pan or zoom, which keeps moving the map smooth on slower phones. Turned on automatically if this device struggles.
settings.konrad_cells_hint: KONRAD3D is the German Weather Service's (DWD) detection and tracking of thunderstorm cells in its radar network. What it draws are not realistic cloud volumes: each cell is its outline on the ground, stacked into tiers sized and raised to a few figures KONRAD3D reports per intensity level. They clash with the 3D map's radar volumes and arrive minutes after the radar, so we suggest leaving this off.
settings.full_resolution_hint: Draws the 3D map at the screen's full resolution. Sharper, but uses more than twice the graphics memory, so on some phones the map may crash and reload.
settings.terrain_hint: Raises the 3D map into the ground's relief and shades its hills, at true scale. Downloads elevation tiles as you move the map.

radar_help.title: How the radar works
radar_help.lede: How the weather radars scan the sky, when they publish what they measured, and which part of meteocool is made from which data.
radar_help.measured: Times are for a German radar cycle, measured on 5 October 2026.

turn.title: One radar, one turn
turn.p1: A weather radar sends a short pulse of microwaves along a narrow beam and then listens. Rain, snow and hail send a small part of it back. The time until the echo returns gives the distance. The strength of the echo gives the reflectivity, measured in dBZ. Stronger echo means heavier rain or hail.
turn.p2: The antenna turns once all the way around. One full turn at one tilt is called a sweep. A German radar cuts each turn into 360 rays, one per degree, and each ray into short pieces of 250 m called bins. Every bin gets one value.
turn.caption: Top view of one sweep. The blue line is the beam as the antenna turns. The coloured areas are echoes, that is water in the air, as rain, snow or hail, sending part of the pulse back. The dashed rings show the distance from the radar. This sweep is one of the low tilts, so it reaches 180 km.
turn.ray: One ray, close up (at about 120 km)
turn.bin: each box is one bin: 250 m along the ray, 1° across
turn.colour: its colour is the echo strength measured there
turn.fact_rays_sub: one per degree of the turn
turn.fact_sweep_sub: at one tilt, roughly 25 to 30 s

tilts.title: Ten tilts make one volume
tilts.p1: After each turn the antenna tilts up or down and turns again. DWD's radars use ten tilts: 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5, 5.5, 8, 12, 17 and 25 degrees. Together they are the volume scan. Only with all ten can you see how high a storm reaches and whether its core leans.
tilts.reach: How far a sweep reaches depends on its tilt. The low tilts, up to 5.5°, reach 180 km. The 8° tilt reaches 124 km, and the steep tilts only 60 km.
tilts.p2: The earth curves away under the beam. Even the lowest tilt is 3.5 km above the ground at 180 km, so far from a radar it misses rain that falls from low clouds. The beam also gets wider: it is 1° wide, which is 3 km at 180 km. And right above the radar there is a cone where no tilt looks.
tilts.p3: A storm far from one radar is often close to another. That is why meteocool fills each 3D cloud from every radar that reaches it, from any country.
tilts.caption: Side view of the ten tilts, drawn to scale with the usual 4/3 earth radius for the bending of the beam. Heights are stretched about five times compared to distance. The low tilts reach 180 km, 8° stops at 124 km, and 12°, 17° and 25° stop at 60 km (the dot on the 12° beam). The storm at 85 km is cut by the six lowest tilts; the 8° beam already passes over its top.
tilts.width: the 0.5° beam is 1° wide: 3 km wide at 180 km

cycle.title: Five minutes, minute by minute
cycle.p1: Every German radar starts a new cycle every five minutes, at :00, :05, :10 and so on. A cycle is named after the minute it starts. Inside a cycle the order is always the same.
cycle.p2: First comes the precipitation scan. It is one low sweep that follows the terrain, and it takes about 30 seconds. DWD makes the flat radar map from this scan, which is why the map is out early.
cycle.p3: Then come the ten tilts of the volume scan, in this order: 5.5, 4.5, 3.5, 2.5, 1.5 and 0.5, then 8, 12, 17 and 25. The 0.5° sweep is done about three minutes into the cycle. The 25° sweep ends at about five minutes, just as the next cycle starts. Each sweep file reaches EUMETNET's public bucket of raw radar data about two minutes after it is scanned.
cycle.caption: One cycle starting at T. Top row: what the antenna does. Middle row: when DWD's files and the raw sweeps appear. Bottom row: when meteocool shows them.
cycle.gap: about 4 minutes between the frame and its clouds

times.note: meteocool times are medians over a day. DWD times are when its files appeared, over several cycles.

made.title: What meteocool makes from which
made.caption: The orange lines are the 3D clouds. A column maximum says where the storms are: DMAX for Germany, meteocool's own for the other countries. The raw sweeps fill each storm's box.
made.de_how: Drawn as map tiles every five minutes. Ready about 2.7 minutes after the scan.
made.forecast_how: DWD's nowcast, 24 steps of five minutes. Push alerts are decided from it too.
made.types_how: DWD's precipitation type. meteocool traces the snow areas from it.
made.networks: Radar map, CH FR CZ PL
made.networks_how: meteocool takes the lowest tilt of each radar, removes speckle and builds one composite per country. It looks for new sweeps every 30 seconds. Ready about 1 minute (Czechia) to 6 minutes (Poland) after the scan.
made.europe_how: All five networks' lowest tilts on one grid, every five minutes. Only shown when chosen in the radar product picker.
made.colmax_how: The strongest echo above each point, from every tilt of all five networks' radars, evened out across them: one five-minute cycle, within 180 km of a radar, up to 12 km. Once a cycle, a scan or two behind. Only shown when chosen in the radar product picker.
made.cells_how: DWD's cell detection and tracking. For each cell meteocool cuts the real outline at each strength out of DMAX.
made.clouds_from: DMAX or meteocool's column maximum, plus raw sweeps
made.clouds_how: The column maximum says where the storms are. For each storm meteocool fills a box with the sweeps of every radar that reaches it, older sweeps counting less. A storm the radars saw well enough can be cut open.
made.lightning_how: Strikes arrive one at a time and appear at once. The lightning tiles are rebuilt every five minutes.

why.title: Why the 3D clouds trail the flat radar
why.p1: The flat map comes from the precipitation scan, which is done half a minute into the cycle. A 3D cloud needs all ten tilts, and the last one ends five minutes into the cycle. So the clouds for a cycle cannot appear before about six minutes, while that cycle's flat frame is out after less than three.
